q: Which fields does a doubly linked list node contain?
e: Each node stores data plus two pointers: prev and next.

q: True or False: A doubly linked list node has two pointers.
e: prev and next are the two pointers.

q: Time complexity of insertion at the beginning?
e: Only a few pointer updates are needed, no traversal.

q: True or False: In a DLL, the first node's prev is NULL.
e: NULL marks the start of the list.

q: Which pointer makes backward traversal possible?
e: prev points to the previous node.

q: What happens if head is NULL?
e: head->prev dereferences NULL. Always check if (head != NULL) first.

q: To delete a middle node t, which two statements reconnect its neighbours?
e: Both neighbours must skip over t before you free it.

q: Insert at the end WITHOUT a tail pointer takes:
e: You must walk to the last node first.

q: True or False: A DLL uses less memory than a singly linked list.
e: The extra prev pointer costs more memory.

q: Which application commonly uses a DLL?
e: You move to the previous or next page, just like prev/next.

q: Insert newNode after temp. What should be done FIRST so the rest of the list is not lost?
e: Save the link to the following node before changing temp->next.

q: True or False: After removing a node you should call free() on it.
e: free() releases memory and prevents a memory leak.

q: List 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30 with tail at 30. What is printed?
code:
t = tail;
while (t) { printf("%d ", t->data); t = t->prev; }
e: Backward traversal visits 30, 20, 10, then NULL stops the loop.
